sections.heading: Auth Systems
sections.text:
EVtivity has two separate authentication systems:

| System | Token Contents | Transport | Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| Operator | `userId`, `roleId` | `csms_token` HTTP-only cookie (or `Authorization` Bearer for API keys) | CSMS dashboard access |
| Driver | `driverId`, `type: 'driver'` | `portal_token` HTTP-only cookie | Driver portal access |

Both realms share one JWT signing key but the server rejects driver tokens on operator routes and operator tokens on driver routes by inspecting the payload shape. A stolen driver JWT cannot be replayed against an operator endpoint and vice versa.

sections.heading: Operator Login
sections.text:
Operators authenticate with email and password. If MFA is enabled, a second factor is required after password verification.

The server sets the JWT in the `csms_token` HTTP-only cookie and a paired `csms_refresh` cookie for refresh-token rotation. The response body also includes the access token for backward compatibility with integration tests and Bearer-only clients.

sections.heading: Driver Login
sections.text: Drivers authenticate with email and password. SMS is available as an MFA second factor, not as a primary login method. Driver JWTs land in the `portal_token` HTTP-only cookie (path `/v1/portal`), with a `portal_refresh` cookie for rotation and a `portal_csrf` cookie for double-submit CSRF protection.

sections.heading: API Keys
sections.text:
API keys provide programmatic access to the REST API.

- Created per user through the CSMS settings UI.
- Sent as a Bearer token in the `Authorization` header.
- Inherits the creating user's role and permissions.
- Supports optional permission scoping to restrict access below the creator's level.
- Creating a key, or widening the permissions of a key, from a signed-in session needs a fresh proof, the same as adding a sign-in method: a code of your current second factor or a passkey, else your current password. An SSO account without a second factor signs in again with SSO. A request made with an API key needs no proof.
- Cannot use the account routes of the signed-in user: profile, password, MFA, notification preferences, and personal AI configuration. These answer 403 `SESSION_REQUIRED`.
- Revoked when the user is deactivated or deleted.

sections.heading: Role-Based Access Control
sections.text:
EVtivity uses 66 granular permissions in `resource:action` format (e.g., `stations:write`, `sessions:read`): 44 page permissions and 22 settings permissions.

Route middleware enforces permissions:

```typescript
authorize('stations:write')
```

Write permission implies read. A user with `stations:write` can also read station data.

Each user holds any subset of the 66 permissions. The system ships with three roles (Admin, Operator, Viewer). A user's role sets their default permissions, and you can then customize the permissions of each user.

sections.heading: Multi-Factor Authentication
sections.text:
Operators and drivers can protect their sign-in with a second factor:

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| Email | One-time code sent to the account's email address |
| TOTP | Time-based one-time password from an authenticator app |
| SMS | One-time code sent by text message through Twilio |
| Passkey or security key | A passkey on a phone, computer or password manager, or a FIDO2 security key such as a YubiKey |
| Recovery code | One of ten single-use codes, for when the other factor is lost |

An account has one code method (email, TOTP or SMS) and up to 20 passkeys and security keys. An admin switches each method on or off for everyone in Settings > Security > MFA (see MFA settings). Operators set up their factors on their Profile, drivers in the portal under Account > Security.

sections.heading: MFA Verification
sections.text:
When a user with MFA enabled submits correct credentials, the server returns a short-lived `mfaPending` JWT (3 minutes) instead of a session. The client posts the code plus the pending JWT to `/v1/auth/mfa/verify` (operator) or `/v1/portal/auth/mfa/verify` (driver). On success the server issues the real session JWT and refresh cookies. The verify routes also take a recovery code (`recoveryCode`) instead of a code, and a passkey or security key goes through `/v1/auth/webauthn/options` and `/verify` (operators) or `/v1/portal/auth/webauthn/options` and `/verify` (drivers). A password change, a password reset or a sign-out between the two steps ends the pending JWT: the API returns 401 `MFA_TOKEN_EXPIRED`.

The email/SMS challenge row stores `(user_id | driver_id, code_hash, expires_at, used_at)`. Verification requires three conditions: the supplied code matches `code_hash` under a constant-time compare, the challenge has not expired or been used, and the challenge's owner matches the principal in the `mfaPending` JWT. The owner check blocks an attacker who has victim A's password but no inbox access from completing login as A by submitting an MFA code from a challenge that belongs to their own account.

A challenge is single-use: a successful verify stamps `used_at`, and subsequent attempts return `MFA_CODE_INVALID`. Per-challenge rate limiting caps failed attempts at five before returning `MFA_CHALLENGE_EXHAUSTED` and forcing the user to request a new code. A code confirms only what it was sent for: a sign-in code never confirms a security change, an email code never confirms SMS, and an SMS code confirms only the number it went to.

sections.heading: MFA Verification
sections.text:
Each operator and driver account gets at most 5 email or SMS codes in 15 minutes for signing in (sign-in, resend, forced password change and SSO). Codes asked for from a signed-in session (factor proofs, replacing recovery codes, MFA setup and phone changes) have their own 5 in 15 minutes, so they never use up the sign-in codes. SMS codes to one phone number are also capped at 3 an hour:

- A setup or phone change code to a number counts the codes every account sent to that number in the last hour.
- A sign-in, resend or proof code to the account's own confirmed number counts the sign-in and proof codes other accounts sent to that number in the last hour. The account's own codes and other accounts' setup and phone change codes do not count against it.

Over a cap, a setup, resend, proof, recovery code replacement or phone change request returns 429 `MFA_RESEND_LIMITED`. A sign-in over the account cap sends no new code, and the newest code of its method that is still valid works. A sign-in over the phone number cap sends no code.

sections.heading: Switched-Off Methods
sections.text:
Switching a method off in Settings refuses new setups of it with 403 `MFA_METHOD_DISABLED`. It also applies at sign-in:

- An account that has another usable factor, such as recovery codes or a passkey, signs in with that factor. A code of the switched-off method returns 403 `MFA_METHOD_DISABLED`. The MFA step opens on the passkey prompt when the account has a passkey, passkeys are switched on, and the browser supports passkeys on a secure page (HTTPS or localhost). Otherwise, when the account has recovery codes left, it opens on the recovery code input, which shows `Your administrator switched off . Sign in with a recovery code.` An account whose other usable factor is only a passkey, with no recovery codes left, sees the code input when the page is plain HTTP on a host other than localhost or the browser does not support passkeys: a code of the switched-off method still returns 403 `MFA_METHOD_DISABLED`, so the account signs in with its passkey from HTTPS or localhost in a browser that supports passkeys.
- An account whose only factor is the switched-off method proves it once more, then sets up an allowed method before the session starts. The mobile app cannot set up a method: a driver whose only factor is switched off gets 403 `MFA_ENROLLMENT_REQUIRED` there, and the app shows `Your sign-in method was turned off. Set up another one in the driver portal at , then sign in here again.`
- When no method can be set up at all, the account signs in after proving its factor.

sections.heading: Sign-In Lockout
sections.text:
Repeated failed operator and driver sign-ins lock the account for a growing delay, on top of the per-IP rate limits. The first lock comes after 5 failures in a row and lasts 30 seconds. Each further failure doubles it, up to 15 minutes. A successful sign-in resets the count. While the account is locked, a password sign-in answers as for a wrong password.

Wrong MFA codes and recovery codes after the password step follow the same rule with their own count. While locked, the API returns 429 `MFA_LOCKED`. A passkey at the MFA step neither counts toward the lock nor waits for it, since its signature cannot be guessed.

Wrong codes entered from a signed-in session to confirm a security change count separately, so a stolen session cannot lock the owner's sign-in with them. A wrong current password counts toward the password sign-in lock wherever it is entered.

sections.heading: Required MFA
sections.text:
An admin can require MFA for operators in Settings > Security > MFA > Require MFA: Off, All Operators, or Selected Roles (the roles under Roles That Must Use MFA). Require MFA for Drivers does the same for every driver. Both settings are off by default, so no one has to use MFA unless an admin turns one on.

- A covered account without MFA gets no session after the password step. The CSMS or the portal opens Set Up Two-Factor Authentication, and the account is signed in once the setup is confirmed. SSO users, including users that SSO creates on their first sign-in, set up MFA the same way.
- A covered account that is already signed in without MFA keeps its session until its access token expires. That is the sign-in check interval in Session Management: 60 minutes by default, set separately for operators and drivers. At that renewal the session ends, and the account sets up MFA when it signs in again. API keys keep working.
- A covered account cannot turn MFA off or remove its last passkey (409 `MFA_REQUIRED_BY_POLICY`). An admin can still reset its MFA. The account then sets up MFA again at its next sign-in.
- Requiring MFA needs email codes or the authenticator app switched on. When no method can be set up for an account, for example SMS only and no phone number, the sign-in fails with 403 `MFA_SETUP_UNAVAILABLE` and never starts a session without MFA.
- When the MFA settings cannot be read, every required MFA check fails closed: an account without MFA cannot sign in or renew its session, and no one can turn MFA off or remove the last passkey (503 `MFA_POLICY_UNAVAILABLE`). Accounts with MFA sign in as usual.

sections.heading: Required MFA
sections.text: The mobile app cannot set up MFA during sign-in or use a passkey or a recovery code, so a driver who must set up MFA, or whose only factors are a passkey or recovery codes, is told to finish in the portal (403 `MFA_ENROLLMENT_REQUIRED`).

sections.heading: Recovery Codes
sections.text:
Turning MFA on, with a code method or a first passkey, creates ten recovery codes. Each signs in once in place of the second factor.

- The codes show only once. Copy them or download them as a text file, and store them somewhere safe. The server keeps only their hashes.
- At the verification step, choose Use a Recovery Code. The reply says how many codes are left.
- Regenerating the codes replaces all of them. It needs a code of the account's method or a passkey.
- Turning MFA off and an admin MFA reset delete the codes.
- An account that turned MFA on before recovery codes existed has none until it generates them on its Profile or Account > Security page.

sections.heading: Passkeys and Security Keys
sections.text:
Operators add passkeys and FIDO2 security keys on their Profile, drivers in the portal under Account > Security. A security key is a physical key, such as a YubiKey, that you plug in or hold near the device and touch when the browser asks. Passkeys need HTTPS on a domain, or `localhost`. The apps hide every passkey option on other pages, and the portal shows none while `PORTAL_URL` is an IP address.

- A passkey works as the second factor after the password. When an admin turns on Passkey Sign-In, a passkey also signs in on its own and counts as both factors. Passkey sign-in needs user verification, such as a fingerprint, face or PIN, so a security key without a PIN works as a second factor only.
- The first passkey of an account without MFA turns MFA on, signs out the account's other sessions and shows the recovery codes once.
- Any FIDO2 authenticator is accepted. The server keeps only the public key.

The relying party ID is the host of `CSMS_URL` for operators and the host of `PORTAL_URL` for drivers. `WEBAUTHN_RP_ID` sets one ID for both apps:

- It must be the CSMS host or a parent domain of it, otherwise the API does not start.
- The portal uses it only when it is also the portal host or a parent domain of it. Otherwise the portal uses its own host.
- A passkey is bound to its relying party ID. Changing `WEBAUTHN_RP_ID` later makes every registered passkey unusable.

For example, `example.com` serves `csms.example.com` and `portal.example.com`. With `csms.example.com`, operators use `csms.example.com` and drivers use `portal.example.com`. A driver passkey never signs in an operator, and an operator passkey never signs in a driver.

sections.heading: Passkeys and Security Keys
sections.text: Never set `WEBAUTHN_RP_ID` to a parent domain with subdomains that serve user content or that third parties run, for example a domain whose subdomains host customer sites, file uploads or a vendor service. A page on any subdomain of the relying party ID can ask the browser for a passkey sign-in for that ID, so such a subdomain could phish passkey assertions. Use the CSMS host itself, or a parent domain whose every subdomain you control.

sections.heading: Confirming Security Changes
sections.text:
A signed-in session alone cannot change how an account signs in. Each change asks for a fresh proof first.

Adding a passkey, setting up a code method, regenerating recovery codes, changing the phone number and creating an API key need:

- A factor the account holds: a code of its method, sent when the proof field opens, or one of its passkeys.
- The current password, when the account has no factor.
- A new SSO sign-in, for an SSO account without a password or factor. It counts for 10 minutes after the SSO sign-in.

An account with none of these, such as an SSO account after SSO was turned off, cannot add a factor or create an API key until an admin resets its password.

Removing a passkey and turning MFA off need a factor the account holds or one of its recovery codes. The password alone never removes a factor. Removing a passkey or turning MFA off signs out the account's other sessions.

A missing proof, or a proof of another kind, returns 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR` with the accepted kinds in `proofKinds`. Each proof works once.

sections.heading: Phone Number Changes
sections.text:
SMS codes go to the account's phone, so a stolen session must not move them.

- An account with a factor confirms a phone number change first.
- An account that signs in with SMS codes also confirms the new number with a code sent to it, through Send Code to New Number. The number is saved only once confirmed.
- The mobile app cannot send the proof, so it tells drivers to change the number in the portal.
- Phone numbers are stored in international format (E.164). A number without a country code is read as a North American number, and a number that does not parse returns 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR`.

Operators and drivers cannot change their own email address. An admin changes an operator's email on the Users page and a driver's email on the driver page. The previous address gets a notice.

sections.heading: SSO Accounts
sections.text:
An SSO account without a password and without a second factor confirms a security change by signing in again with SSO. This applies to adding a first sign-in method or passkey and to creating an API key. The confirmation lasts 10 minutes after the SSO sign-in.

An SSO sign-in must finish in the browser that started it. The CSMS sets a short-lived binding cookie when the sign-in starts and accepts the identity provider's reply only from the browser that holds it. Otherwise the sign-in page shows that the reply did not match a sign-in started in this browser, and no session starts.

- Over HTTPS the cookie is `__Host-csms_sso_binding`, which no other subdomain can set. With `COOKIE_DOMAIN` set, it is `csms_sso_binding` on that domain, so every subdomain of `COOKIE_DOMAIN` must be one you trust.
- Over plain HTTP, such as local development, Chrome sends the cookie back only within two minutes of the start of the sign-in. Firefox and Safari have no such limit. An identity provider sign-in in Chrome that takes longer must be started again.

sections.heading: TOTP Configuration
sections.text:
- Algorithm: SHA1
- Digits: 6
- Period: 30 seconds
- Window tolerance: 1 step (±30s)
- Each code is accepted once
- QR code generated server-side for authenticator app setup
- Secret stored encrypted at rest (`totp_secret_enc`) and decrypted only at verification time

sections.heading: Security Notices
sections.text:
Operators and drivers get an email when the security of their account changes. An account that signs in with SMS codes also gets a text message. A notice goes out when:

- A sign-in method or passkey is added or removed.
- Two-factor authentication is turned on or off.
- An administrator resets the account's MFA.
- Recovery codes are regenerated, or a recovery code is used.
- The phone number changes. The notice also goes to the previous number.
- An administrator changes the email address. The notice goes to the previous address.
- An operator creates an API key.

Each notice tells the user what to do if they did not make the change. These notices are always on. Edit their templates under Notifications > System Events, in the Account Security group. When drivers turn off two-factor authentication themselves, they get the `driver.MfaDisabled` notice.

sections.heading: reCAPTCHA
sections.text:
EVtivity uses Google reCAPTCHA v3 for bot protection.

- Invisible to users (no checkbox or challenge).
- Score-based with a configurable threshold (default 0.5).
- Enable and configure in Settings > Security.
- The site key, secret key, and threshold are dashboard settings, not environment variables. The secret key is stored encrypted.
- Turn it on when anyone can sign up in the driver portal. It protects the portal sign-in, sign-up, forgot password and reset password forms, and the guest charging start. The mobile apps prove themselves with device attestation instead.
- While it is off, those forms are protected only by IP rate limits, and Settings > Security shows a warning.

sections.heading: Driver sign-up limits
sections.text:
These limits apply whether reCAPTCHA is on or off, on top of the IP rate limits:

- The account verification link goes to the driver's email address only, never by SMS.
- A driver gets at most one verification email a minute and five in 24 hours, the sign-up email included. Over the limit, the API returns `VERIFICATION_RESEND_LIMITED`.
- A phone number can be used for at most three portal registrations in 24 hours. Over the limit, the API returns `PHONE_REGISTRATION_LIMITED`. Several drivers can share a phone number.

sections.heading: CSRF Protection
sections.text:
Token-based CSRF protection is active on all mutating requests (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) for cookie-based authentication. This applies to the driver portal, which uses HTTP-only cookies for auth.

API key and Bearer token authentication are not subject to CSRF protection.

sections.heading: Password Policy
sections.text:
One password policy applies to operators and drivers. Admins set it in Settings > Security > Passwords and Sessions. By default a password needs at least 12 characters, an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter and a number. A special character (a printable ASCII character that is not a letter, digit or space) can also be required. The minimum length ranges from 8 to 64, and a new password is at most 128 characters.

- The API checks the policy on every route that sets a new password. A password that misses a rule answers 400 `WEAK_PASSWORD`, and the `missing` list of the body names the rules it misses (`minLength`, `uppercase`, `lowercase`, `number`, `symbol`, `maxLength`). A password under 8 or over 128 characters answers 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR`.
- Sign-in never checks the policy, so a stricter policy locks nobody out. It applies the next time someone sets a password.
- `GET /v1/security/public` (no sign-in) returns the policy in effect as `passwordPolicy` (`minLength`, `requireUppercase`, `requireLowercase`, `requireNumber`, `requireSymbol`), so a client can list the rules.
- `PUT /v1/security/password-policy` sets the five policy fields, and `PUT /v1/security/sessions` sets the four session lifetimes below. Both take every field, need `settings.security:write` and access to all sites. `GET /v1/security/settings` (`settings.security:read`) returns the values in effect as `passwordPolicy` and `sessionLifetimes`.

sections.heading: Session Management
sections.text:
- Access tokens are short-lived JWTs. Their lifetime is the sign-in check interval: 60 minutes by default, from 5 to 1440, set separately for operators (`operatorAccessMinutes`) and drivers (`driverAccessMinutes`). The access cookie lives as long as the token.

- Refresh tokens keep a session signed in without storing credentials. Their lifetime is the inactivity timeout: 30 days by default, from 1 to 90 for operators (`operatorRefreshDays`) and from 1 to 365 for drivers (`driverRefreshDays`). Each rotation starts a new lifetime, so a session ends after that long without use. The refresh cookie and the stored refresh token have the same lifetime.

- A lifetime change applies to tokens issued after it. A refresh issues both tokens with the current values, so an active session takes on the new lifetimes at its next renewal. A session no one uses keeps its old expiry.

- Token rotation: each refresh token is single-use. Using a refresh token issues a new access token and a new refresh token.

- Rotation is enforced atomically. Two concurrent refresh attempts with the same token race on `UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = NOW() WHERE id = X AND revoked_at IS NULL RETURNING id`; only one caller's update returns a row. The loser receives `401 INVALID_REFRESH_TOKEN` rather than silently minting a parallel session.

- Signing out ends the operator session at once. A password change, an MFA change, a role or permission change, and deactivation end every session of the user at once.

- Deactivating or deleting an operator also revokes the user's API keys and emailed links. A password reset link works once.

sections.heading: Session Management
sections.text:
- Operator accounts created through SSO have no password. They cannot sign in with a password, reset it, or change it. A password reset or invitation sent by an operator for such a user returns 409 `USER_SSO_MANAGED`.

- A replayed (already-revoked) refresh token is rejected on the SELECT (`WHERE revoked_at IS NULL`) and returns `401 INVALID_REFRESH_TOKEN`. The legitimate session, having rotated to a new token, continues until natural expiry.

- Logging out revokes the current refresh token immediately and clears the auth cookies. The portal and CSMS frontends both await the logout response before clearing local state so a tab-close race cannot leave the revocation un-applied.

sections.heading: PostgreSQL
sections.text: EVtivity requires PostgreSQL 17.

sections.heading: Default Connection
sections.text:
```bash
postgres://evtivity:evtivity@localhost:5433/evtivity
```

Set via the `DATABASE_URL` environment variable.

sections.heading: Using Docker
sections.text:
The included `docker-compose.yml` runs PostgreSQL on port 5433 (external) mapped to 5432 (internal):

```bash
docker compose up postgres
```

Compose publishes port 5433 on `127.0.0.1` only. To expose it, change the default `evtivity` / `evtivity` login first, then set `INFRA_BIND_IP` in `.env`. See Docker Compose.

pgAdmin is available on port 7109 when you start with the tools profile:

```bash
docker compose --profile tools up
```

sections.heading: Drizzle ORM
sections.text: EVtivity uses Drizzle ORM for schema definition, migrations, and queries.

sections.heading: Schema Organization
sections.text: Schema files live in `packages/database/src/schema/` with 33 files organized by domain (stations, sessions, drivers, billing, notifications, etc.).

sections.heading: Key Conventions
sections.text:
- Primary keys: Nanoid text PKs for user-facing entities with domain prefixes (`sta_`, `ses_`, `drv_`). Serial integers for internal tables.
- Timestamps: All timestamp columns use `timestamp with time zone`.
- Money: Monetary values stored in cents as integers.
- Energy: Energy values stored in watt-hours (Wh) as integers.

sections.heading: Migration Commands
sections.text:
Run these from the repository root:

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `npm run check:migrations` | Check the migrations journal: every SQL file has an entry, indexes are sequential, and timestamps increase |
| `npm run db:migrate` | Apply pending migrations to the database |
| `npm run db:seed` | Seed the database with initial data. Re-running adds only missing settings, roles, and users and keeps existing values, including the admin password. `npm run db:seed -- --apply-config` writes the values from `packages/database/seed.config.json` over existing settings. |

Write each migration by hand. A schema change in `packages/database/src/schema/` needs a migration in the same change: the next numbered, idempotent SQL file in `packages/database/src/migrations/` (guarded statements such as `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`) and its entry in `packages/database/src/migrations/meta/_journal.json`. Do not use `npm run generate`: the Drizzle snapshot baseline is frozen, so it cannot diff the schema correctly. Run `npm run check:migrations`, then `npm run db:migrate`.

sections.heading: Rules
sections.text:
- Never create new `postgres()` connections. Use the shared database client from `@evtivity/database`.
- Never import from another package's schema files directly. Use the re-exports from the database package.

sections.heading: Redis
sections.text:
Redis is required for three purposes:

1. Pub/sub: Inter-service communication between API and OCPP servers, and server-sent events (SSE) to frontends.
2. Job queues: BullMQ handles background jobs (notifications, billing, certificate management).
3. Caching: Session data, rate limiting, and connection registry.

Default connection:

```bash
redis://localhost:6379
```

Set via the `REDIS_URL` environment variable.

Each service connects as its own Redis ACL user (`api`, `ocpp`, `ocpi`, `worker`, `css`) with only the keys, pub/sub channels, and commands it needs. Docker Compose creates the users from `docker/redis/acl-rules.conf` and gives each service its own `REDIS_URL`. The Redis `default` user stays open for tools on the host, so Compose publishes port 6379 on `127.0.0.1` only. Set `REDIS_API_PASSWORD`, `REDIS_OCPP_PASSWORD`, `REDIS_OCPI_PASSWORD`, `REDIS_WORKER_PASSWORD`, and `REDIS_CSS_PASSWORD` to replace the development passwords when the stack runs on a shared host.

sections.heading: Environment Variables
sections.text:
Copy `.env.example` to `.env` at the repo root. The defaults work for local development. Production deployments require you to set secrets and URLs explicitly.

When adding a new environment variable, update all 5 locations: Zod config schema, `.env.example`, `docker-compose.yml`, Helm `values.yaml`, and Helm `configmap.yaml`.

sections.heading: Network
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `BIND_IP` | `0.0.0.0` | IP address to bind the user-facing Docker ports to (CSMS, portal, API, OCPP, OCPP TLS, OCPI). Use `0.0.0.0` for all interfaces (accessible from other machines) or `127.0.0.1` for localhost only. |
| `INFRA_BIND_IP` | `127.0.0.1` | IP address to bind the Docker Compose infrastructure and tool ports to (postgres, pgadmin, mailpit, ftp, prometheus, grafana, loki). They use default logins, so they stay on localhost unless you set `0.0.0.0` or a LAN IP on a trusted network. Redis and the Node inspector (9229) always stay on `127.0.0.1`. |

sections.heading: Database and Redis
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | `postgres://evtivity:evtivity@localhost:5433/evtivity` | PostgreSQL connection string |
| `DB_POOL_MAX` | `20` | Connections each process pools (api, ocpp, ocpi, worker; the simulator defaults to `10`). Keep the sum over all processes below the PostgreSQL `max_connections` (docker-compose sets `200`). The OCPP server authenticates at most half its pool of station connections at once. |
| `REDIS_URL` | `redis://localhost:6379` | Redis connection string for pub/sub, queues, and caching. In Docker Compose, Helm, and AWS each service connects as its own ACL user (`redis://:@host:6379`) |
| `REDIS_TLS_CA_PEM` | - | CA certificate (PEM) that signed the Redis server certificate, for a `rediss://` URL with a private CA. The Helm chart sets it when `redisTls.enabled` |
| `REDIS_TLS_CA_FILE` | - | Path to that CA certificate, as an alternative to `REDIS_TLS_CA_PEM` |
| `SEED_DEMO` | `false` | Read by `npm run db:seed`. Set to `true` to populate demo data (stations, sessions, drivers) when seeding. When `false`, only settings, roles, and the admin user are created. The migrate container does not auto-seed; seeding is always explicit. |
| `SEED_CSS_TARGET_URL` | `ws://ocpp:7103` | Override for the OCPP URL written to simulator station rows by the demo seed, as reachable from the simulator container. |
| `SEED_CSS_TLS_TARGET_URL` | `wss://ocpp:8443` | TLS variant of the seeded simulator target URL. |
| `REGISTRATION_POLICY` | `approval-required` | Station onboarding policy at first install. `approval-required` or `open`. Change later via dashboard, API, or Helm. |

sections.heading: Initial Seed Credentials
sections.text:
Created by the migrate container's seed steps on first `docker compose up -d`. Idempotent: subsequent runs do not overwrite existing rows. Override these before bringing up the stack in any non-local environment.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAIL` | `admin@evtivity.local` | Email for the initial admin user |
| `INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | `admin123` | Password for the initial admin user |
| `INITIAL_ADMIN_MUST_RESET_PASSWORD` | `false` | Force a password change on the admin's first login |

sections.text:
| `TRUST_PROXY` | - | API and OCPI. Comma-separated IP addresses or CIDR ranges of the proxies or load balancers in front of the service. The service then takes the client address from their `X-Forwarded-For` (and the scheme from `X-Forwarded-Proto`), so rate limits, the guest charging limits per IP address, and audit and access logs see the real client behind a load balancer or ingress. The API refuses to start on an IP address, a single label other than `localhost`, a value that does not cover the CSMS host, or any value while the CSMS host is an IP address. sections.heading: Protocol Support
sections.text: EVtivity supports OCPP 1.6, OCPP 2.0.1 and OCPP 2.1. All three subprotocols (`ocpp1.6`, `ocpp2.0.1`, `ocpp2.1`) are accepted on the same WebSocket server. The server picks the protocol version from the subprotocol header during the WebSocket handshake. When a station offers more than one, the server prefers 2.1, then 2.0.1, then 1.6.

sections.heading: OCPP 2.0.1 stations
sections.text:
OCPP 2.0.1 stations share the OCPP 2.x model with 2.1 stations: EVSEs, `TransactionEvent`, the device model, display messages, monitoring, certificates and smart charging work the same way. Every message the CSMS sends to a 2.0.1 station is checked against the OCPP 2.0.1 schema before it is sent.

These OCPP 2.1 features are not available on OCPP 2.0.1 stations:

- Tariffs and cost calculation on the station, including the tariff in the `Authorize` response
- Transaction limits sent to the station (maximum cost, energy or time)
- DER control
- Bidirectional charging (V2X)
- Battery swap
- Priority charging
- Periodic event streams
- Web payments (dynamic QR codes) and ad hoc payments
- ISO 15118-20 certificates
- The CALLRESULTERROR and SEND message types

A command that uses one of these features, or a value OCPP 2.0.1 does not define, is refused with `400 OCPP_VERSION_MISMATCH` and nothing is sent to the station.

sections.heading: Connection URL
Security Profiles
sections.text:
| Profile | Auth Method | Port | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| No Auth | None | 7103 | No authentication. Development only. |
| Basic Auth | Basic Auth | 7103 | Username is stationId, password is a hash stored in the station record. |
| TLS + Basic Auth | TLS | 8443 | Server-side TLS. Station validates the server certificate. |
| Mutual TLS | Mutual TLS | 8443 | Client certificate required. Both sides validate certificates. |

TLS + Basic Auth and Mutual TLS share the same TLS port. The server is configured with `requestCert: true` and `rejectUnauthorized: false`, allowing it to accept both TLS + Basic Auth (no client cert) and Mutual TLS (with client cert) connections on a single port.

sections.heading: TLS Configuration
sections.text:
Set these environment variables to enable the TLS listener:

```bash
OCPP_TLS_PORT=8443
OCPP_TLS_CERT=/path/to/server.crt
OCPP_TLS_KEY=/path/to/server.key
OCPP_TLS_CA=/path/to/ca.crt
```

sections.heading: Connection Limits
sections.text:
| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `OCPP_MAX_CONNECTIONS_PER_IP` | `2500` | Max concurrent WebSocket connections from a single IP |
| `OCPP_MAX_MESSAGES_PER_IP_PER_SECOND` | `5000` | Message rate limit per IP |
| `OCPP_AUTH_MAX_CONCURRENT` | Half of `DB_POOL_MAX` | Station connections authenticated at once |
| `OCPP_AUTH_MAX_QUEUED` | `1000` | Station connections waiting for authentication. `0` turns the queue off. |
| `OCPP_AUTH_MAX_WAIT_MS` | `10000` | Longest wait in the queue, in milliseconds |

Connections from one IP that are still authenticating count toward `OCPP_MAX_CONNECTIONS_PER_IP`. Over the limit, the server answers 429 before it looks up the station.

sections.heading: Connection admission
sections.text:
The OCPP server admits a reconnect wave, such as one after a restart, without starving the stations already connected:

- Station connections wait in a queue for authentication. When the queue is full or the wait is too long, the server answers 503 with a `Retry-After` header, and the station retries after its back-off.
- A successful password check is cached for 15 minutes in each OCPP server process. A password change clears it, and so does a security profile change saved for an offline station.
- Password checks run on a limited number of CPU threads, so DNS, compression, and other work keep a thread.
- When a stored password hash uses older hash parameters, the server admits the station first and updates the hash in the background.

To admit more stations at once, raise `DB_POOL_MAX` rather than `OCPP_AUTH_MAX_CONCURRENT`. The rest of the pool serves the messages of connected stations.

sections.heading: Failed login throttling
sections.text: After 5 wrong passwords for one station within 60 seconds, the server refuses that station for 60 seconds with HTTP 429 and a `Retry-After` header, without checking the password. See Stations.

sections.heading: Configurable Settings
sections.text:
These are configured through the CSMS settings UI, not environment variables:

- Heartbeat interval: Default 300 seconds. Sent to stations in BootNotification response.
- Offline command queue TTL: Default 24 hours. Commands queued for offline stations expire after this duration.

sections.heading: Message Pipeline
sections.text:
Inbound OCPP messages pass through a middleware pipeline:

1. Rate limit - enforces per-IP message rate
2. Log - records the raw message
3. Validate - validates against the OCPP JSON schema
4. Route - dispatches to the appropriate handler

sections.heading: Command Flow
sections.text:
OCPP commands from the API to a station follow this path:

```bash
API -> Redis pub/sub (ocpp_commands channel) -> CommandListener -> WebSocket -> Station
```

The API publishes the command to Redis. The OCPP server instance holding the station connection picks it up via the CommandListener and sends it over the WebSocket.

sections.heading: Event Projections
sections.text: Inbound OCPP messages trigger domain event projections that update database state: station status, connector status, active sessions, meter values, and running costs.

sections.heading: Horizontal Scaling
sections.text:
To run multiple OCPP server instances:

1. Set `OCPP_INSTANCE_ID` on each instance. In Kubernetes, use the pod name.
2. The `RedisConnectionRegistry` tracks which station is connected to which instance.
3. Commands are routed through Redis pub/sub. The instance holding the target station connection receives and forwards the command.

Each instance subscribes to both the global `ocpp_commands` channel and its own instance-specific channel.

sections.heading: Per-process health
sections.text:
Each OCPP server process reports its own health: its connected stations and its ping figures. The dashboard OCPP and Infrastructure cards add up all processes, so the connected station count covers every OCPP server. A process that stops drops out of the totals.

The API exports these values to Prometheus on its metrics port:

| Metric | Description |
|---|---|
| `ocpp_connected_stations` | Stations connected to all OCPP servers |
| `ocpp_instances` | OCPP server processes reporting health |
| `ocpp_instance_connected_stations{ocpp_instance}` | Stations connected to one OCPP server process |
| `ocpp_ping_latency_avg_ms`, `ocpp_ping_latency_max_ms` | Average and highest ping latency |
| `ocpp_ping_success_rate` | Share of successful pings |

Every API process exports the same values. Aggregate them across API processes with `max()`, or `max by (ocpp_instance)` for the per-process series, never with `sum()`.

The Grafana "System Metrics" dashboard shows them in its "OCPP Health" row: "Connected Stations", "Avg Ping Latency", "Max Ping Latency", "Ping Success Rate", "Connected Stations Over Time", and "Ping Latency Over Time". "Connected Stations Over Time" has an "All" series plus one series per OCPP server (pod name or ECS task). The dashboard also has the "Overview", "HTTP", "Node.js Runtime", and "Process" rows.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
These are the OCTT test cases for the charge point role in OCPP 1.6. The test runner acts as a Central System and checks how the EVtivity Charging Station Simulator behaves. See OCPP Conformance Testing for how tests run and how results are counted.

Modules follow the numbered sections of the OCPP 1.6 test case document. A suffix such as `_1` or `_2` on a test ID marks a variant of the same test case.

sections.heading: PICS
sections.text: The simulator declares these rows of the OCPP 1.6 PICS. It supports every row, so every test case applies.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
These are the OCTT test cases for the charging station role in OCPP 2.0.1 (Edition 4, Part 6). The test runner acts as a CSMS, runs the Charging Station Simulator as an OCPP 2.0.1 station, and checks how it behaves. See OCPP Conformance Testing for how tests run and how results are counted.

A test case applies only when the simulator's PICS meets its conditions. The PICS section lists every item, and the Not applicable section lists every excluded test case.

sections.heading: PICS
sections.text: OCPP 2.0.1 Part 5 (Certification Profiles) gives these test cases the same conditions as OCPP 2.1 Part 5, so the simulator declares the same items for both versions, with two differences. QR code payment (`P-2.4`) is not supported on OCPP 2.0.1, because its test case needs messages that exist only in OCPP 2.1. The simulator supports every OCPP 2.0.1 display message state, so the item for a station that lacks one (`UnsupportedDisplayMessageState`) is not supported and TC_O_18_CS does not apply. An unsupported item excludes every test case that needs it. A supported item excludes the test cases that need a station without it.

sections.heading: Not applicable
sections.text: The simulator's PICS excludes these test cases. They are not run and do not count as passed.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
These are the OCTT test cases for the charging station role in OCPP 2.1. The test runner acts as a CSMS and checks how the EVtivity Charging Station Simulator behaves. See OCPP Conformance Testing for how tests run and how results are counted.

A test case applies only when the simulator's PICS meets its conditions. The PICS section lists every item, and the Not applicable section lists every excluded test case.

sections.heading: PICS
sections.text: The simulator declares these items from OCPP 2.1 Part 5 (Certification Profiles). Items without a Part 5 ID come from a test case prerequisite in the OCTT test case document. An unsupported item excludes every test case that needs it. A supported item excludes the test cases that need a station without it.

sections.heading: Not applicable
sections.text: The simulator's PICS excludes these test cases. They are not run and do not count as passed.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
These are the OCTT test cases for the Central System role in OCPP 1.6, run against the EVtivity CSMS. The test runner acts as a charge point and checks how the CSMS responds. See OCPP Conformance Testing for how tests run and how results are counted.

OCPP 1.6 test cases use numeric IDs such as `TC_003_CSMS`. A suffix such as `_1` or `_2` marks a variant of the same test case.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
These are the OCTT test cases for the CSMS role in OCPP 2.0.1 (Edition 4, Part 6). The test runner acts as a charging station that connects over the `ocpp2.0.1` subprotocol and checks how the EVtivity CSMS responds. See OCPP Conformance Testing for how tests run and how results are counted.

This is a self-run conformance check: EVtivity runs its own implementation of the Open Charge Alliance test cases. It is not an Open Charge Alliance certificate. It shows how the CSMS performs on the test cases that an official certification test uses.

sections.heading: Results by certification profile
sections.text: OCPP 2.0.1 Part 5 (Certification Profiles) lists each test case in one or more profiles: Core, Advanced Security, Smart Charging, and ISO 15118 Support. Within a profile, a test case is mandatory or conditional. Test cases that Part 6 defines but no profile lists are informative. A test case listed in more than one profile counts in each.

sections.heading: Not applicable
sections.text: These test cases need a feature EVtivity does not include. They are not run and do not count as passed.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: These are the OCTT test cases for the CSMS role in OCPP 2.1. The test runner acts as a charging station and checks how the EVtivity CSMS responds. See OCPP Conformance Testing for how tests run and how results are counted.

sections.heading: Not applicable
sections.text: These test cases need a feature EVtivity does not include. They are not run and do not count as passed.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
The Open Charge Alliance (OCA) publishes the OCPP Compliance Testing Tool (OCTT) test cases. Each OCPP version has one set of test cases for the CSMS role and one for the charging station role. A test case has an ID such as `TC_B_01_CSMS`, prerequisites, and a step-by-step message sequence with expected results.

EVtivity includes its own test runner that implements these test cases. It runs six suites:

Pending counts every applicable test that does not pass yet. Open a suite for the per-module results and the status of every test case.

These results come from the EVtivity test runner, which follows the OCTT test case specifications. They are a self-run conformance check, not an Open Charge Alliance certification.

sections.heading: What gets tested
sections.text:
| Suite | Runner acts as | System under test |
|-------|----------------|-------------------|
| CSMS | A charging station. It connects to the OCPP WebSocket server, sends station messages, and checks every CSMS response. Tests that need a CSMS-initiated command trigger it through the REST API, the same way an operator does. | The EVtivity CSMS (OCPP server, API, and worker) |
| Charging station | A CSMS. It starts a test OCPP server for each test case, connects a Charging Station Simulator to it, sends CSMS commands, and checks the station's messages and behavior. | The EVtivity Charging Station Simulator |

Tests follow the OCTT documents step by step. A test only calls a physical station action (plug in, present a card, power cycle) where the OCTT test case lists a manual action.

The OCPP 2.0.1 suites run the OCPP 2.0.1 test cases. Each one has an OCPP 2.1 test case with the same ID and scenario, so the runner runs that test case over the `ocpp2.0.1` subprotocol. The OCPP 2.0.1 CSMS results also show the counts per certification profile.

In the charging station suites, the runner checks every message in both directions against the strict OCPP JSON schemas of the version under test. A message with a field or value the version does not define, or without a required field, fails the test case.

sections.heading: How results are counted
sections.text:
| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| Passed | Every step checked a real condition and got the expected result. |
| Not applicable | The test case does not apply to the product. It is not run and does not count as passed. |
| Pending | The test case applies but does not pass yet. |
| Failed | A step got a result other than the expected one. |
| Error | The test could not finish, for example a connection error or a timeout. |
| Skipped | The test case applies but could not run in this setup, for example a TLS step without a TLS server URL. |

sections.heading: Not applicable for the charging station
sections.text:
Real OCTT runs only the test cases that the vendor's PICS (Protocol Implementation Conformance Statement) makes applicable. The EVtivity runner does the same with the simulator's PICS. OCPP 2.1 and 2.0.1 items use the IDs from Part 5 (Certification Profiles), such as `ISO15118Support`, `C-13`, or `SC-6`. OCPP 1.6 items follow the rows of the OCPP 1.6 PICS.

A test case lists the PICS items it needs. Some test cases need a product without a feature. For example, TC_B_28_CS applies only to a station that cannot reset a single EVSE. The simulator supports reset per EVSE, so TC_B_25_CS to TC_B_27_CS run instead. When a condition is not met, the runner reports the test as not applicable with the PICS item and the reason.

An item is only declared unsupported when the simulator lacks the feature. The PICS tables on the OCPP 2.1 charging station, OCPP 2.0.1 charging station and OCPP 1.6 charging station pages list every item and why it is or is not supported.

sections.heading: Not applicable for the CSMS
sections.text: A CSMS test case is not applicable when it needs a feature EVtivity does not include. Each one names the missing feature on the results page.

sections.heading: Test isolation
sections.text:
- Each CSMS test gets its own test station and its own ID tokens (valid, blocked, expired, prepaid, and others). Tests that run in parallel never share a token.
- After each test, the runner stops any transaction the test left open, as the OCTT test procedure requires.
- When the run ends, the runner deletes its test stations, test driver, tokens, and temporary API key, and restores the settings it changed.
- Each charging station test gets its own test server on an ephemeral port on `127.0.0.1`, so parallel tests never collide.

Run conformance tests against a development or test deployment. The runner writes test stations, tokens, and settings to the CSMS database while it runs.

sections.heading: Run tests from the dashboard
sections.text:
1. Open Settings in the CSMS sidebar and select the Conformance tab.
2. In System Under Test, choose CSMS or Charging Station Simulator.
3. Choose OCPP 2.1, OCPP 2.0.1, OCPP 1.6, or Run All Tests.
4. Click Run Tests. The worker runs the suite and the run list updates in real time.
5. Click a run to see the per-module breakdown and the expected and actual result of every step.

The dashboard runs the CSMS suites without a TLS server URL or an OCSP responder. Tests that need either one report the affected steps as skipped. Use the command line for a full CSMS run. A charging station run needs no running CSMS: the worker starts its own test servers and simulator stations. See Conformance Testing for the dashboard pages.

sections.heading: Run CSMS tests from the command line
sections.text:
Run these commands from the CSMS repository root. The runner reads `DATABASE_URL` from `.env` and needs the OCPP server, API, and database running.

```bash
# All CSMS tests, every version
npm run octt

# One version
npm run octt:2.1
npm run octt:1.6
npm run octt -- --version ocpp2.0.1

# One module
npx tsx packages/octt/src/cli.ts --server ws://localhost:7103 --version ocpp2.1 --module E-transactions

# Full OCPP 2.1 run with the TLS and OCSP steps
npx tsx packages/octt/src/cli.ts --server ws://localhost:7103 --version ocpp2.1 \
  --tls-server wss://localhost:8443 \
  --ocsp-responder http://host.docker.internal:8090/ocsp
```

| Flag | Default | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| `--server` | `ws://localhost:7103` | OCPP WebSocket URL of the CSMS |
| `--tls-server` | none | `wss://` URL of the CSMS TLS listener. Tests that reconnect over TLS (security profile upgrades, TC_A_19_CSMS) need it. Without it those steps are skipped. |
| `--ocsp-responder` | none | URL of a test OCSP responder the runner starts, for example `http://host.docker.internal:8090/ocsp`. The OCPP server must reach it. Contract certificate and OCSP tests (TC_C_50 to TC_C_52, TC_M_24) need it. Without it they are skipped. |
| `--version` | all | `ocpp2.1`, `ocpp2.0.1` or `ocpp1.6` |
| `--module` | all | One module, for example `B-provisioning` (2.1) or `core` (1.6) |
| `--concurrency` | `10` | Number of tests that run in parallel |
| `--api-url` | `http://localhost:7102` | REST API URL used to trigger CSMS-initiated commands |
| `--password` | none | Basic Auth password for the test stations |

sections.heading: Run CSMS tests from the command line
sections.text: When the OCSP responder runs on a private host such as `host.docker.internal`, add that host to the CSMS setting `pnc.ocsp.allowedPrivateHosts`. The runner installs a test MO root certificate for the run and removes it at the end.

sections.heading: Run charging station tests from the command line
sections.text:
The charging station runner starts its own test servers and Charging Station Simulator instances. It needs the database but not a running CSMS. It uses the built simulator package, so build it after you change the simulator.

```bash
# Build the simulator
npx tsc -b packages/css

# All charging station tests, every version
npm run octt:cs

# One version
npm run octt:cs:2.1
npm run octt:cs:1.6
npx tsx packages/octt/src/cs-cli.ts --version ocpp2.0.1

# One module
npx tsx packages/octt/src/cs-cli.ts --version ocpp2.1 --module E-transactions

# Selected test cases
npx tsx packages/octt/src/cs-cli.ts --version ocpp2.1 --test-ids TC_E_01_CS,TC_E_02_CS
```

| Flag | Default | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| `--version` | all | `ocpp2.1`, `ocpp2.0.1` or `ocpp1.6` |
| `--module` | all | One module, for example `K-smart-charging` (2.1 and 2.0.1) or `21-reservation` (1.6) |
| `--test-ids` | all | Comma-separated test case IDs |
| `--concurrency` | `3` | Number of tests that run in parallel |

The output prints one line per test: `[PASS]`, `[FAIL]`, `[SKIP]`, `[ERR ]`, or `[N/A ]` with the PICS reason. The summary adds a `Not applicable (PICS)` count.

sections.heading: Results pages
sections.text:
- OCPP 2.1 CSMS
- OCPP 2.0.1 CSMS
- OCPP 1.6 CSMS
- OCPP 2.1 Charging Station
- OCPP 2.0.1 Charging Station
- OCPP 1.6 Charging Station

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: The Access Logs page captures every authenticated request and background job run across the platform. Four tabs split the data by source so you can investigate one surface at a time without sifting through unrelated traffic.

sections.heading: Tabs
sections.text:
- CSMS — operator dashboard requests authenticated with a session cookie.
- Portal — driver portal requests authenticated with a driver session cookie.
- API — all `/v1/*` requests, including both session-authenticated and API-key-authenticated calls. Use the Method and Status filters to narrow results.
- Workers — background job runs from the BullMQ worker. Filter by queue (`cron-jobs`, `load-management`, `guest-session-events`) or status (`started`, `completed`, `failed`).

Server-sent event streams (`/v1/events/stream`) are excluded so long-lived connections don't flood the table.

sections.heading: Log Fields
sections.text:
Each row records timestamp, user (or API key name on the API tab), action or path, HTTP method and status (API tab), and duration. Click a row to expand the request IP address, user agent, and request body when one was captured.

The Workers tab shows job name, queue, start time, duration, and the full error stack when a job failed.

sections.heading: Sensitive Data
sections.text:
The notification dispatcher redacts sensitive content before persisting it to the notification history. Six-digit verification codes and `token`, `code`, `verifyToken`, `verificationToken`, `magicToken`, `resetToken`, and `otp` query parameters are replaced with `` in:

- `mfa.*` events (TOTP setup confirmations, SMS and email verification codes)
- `driver.ForgotPassword` and `operator.ForgotPassword` (reset links)
- `driver.AccountVerification` (email verification links)
- `driver.Welcome` (initial verification link)

The redaction applies to both subject and body fields. Other operator emails and audit log entries are unaffected.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.text:
Each log table has its own retention setting so noisy operational tables can stay short while security-critical history is preserved longer.

| Setting | Default | Table |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `logs.access.retentionDays` | 30 | Access logs (CSMS, Portal, API tabs) |
| `logs.ocppMessage.retentionDays` | 30 | OCPP message log |
| `logs.connection.retentionDays` | 90 | Connection log |
| `logs.notifications.retentionDays` | 90 | Notification history |
| `logs.securityEvents.retentionDays` | 365 | Security events |
| `logs.portStatus.retentionDays` | 30 | Connector status history |
| `logs.workerJob.retentionDays` | 30 | Worker job logs (Workers tab) |

A daily cron job named `log-retention-prune` runs at 03:30 UTC and removes rows older than each setting's cutoff in 1000-row batches so a large prune does not hold an exclusive lock. Set any value to 0 to disable pruning for that table.

The audit log family (per-entity History tabs and the global Audit page) is governed separately by `audit.retentionDays`. See Audit Logs for details.

sections.heading: API Access
sections.text: `GET /v1/access-logs` returns the same data the CSMS, Portal, and API tabs render. `GET /v1/worker-logs` powers the Workers tab. Both require the `logs:read` permission. See the API reference for query parameters.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
The AI assistant answers questions about your charging network in plain language. It reads live data through the CSMS API with your own permissions and site access, so it sees only what you can see. It can also propose changes, but it never runs one until you confirm it.

The assistant is one of the AI features of the CSMS:

- Automatic insights: root-cause notes about offline or faulted stations, failed sessions, refused authorizations, and reservation problems, and background worker suggestions with an action you confirm.
- Background AI workers: optional scheduled jobs that summarize the network and find stuck sessions and tariff anomalies.
- AI usage and budgets: token usage and budgets.
- MCP server: connects AI agents to EVtivity with an API key.

The assistant works with four AI providers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, and DeepSeek. An administrator adds the provider keys in Settings > AI > Providers and Keys. The assistant itself is set up in Settings > AI > Assistant (see Settings).

The conversation text, the data the assistant reads, and attached files are sent to the selected AI provider. This data leaves your deployment. Check the provider's data retention terms before you turn the assistant on.

What the AI Provider Receives

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: The AI provider never receives stored credentials, such as passwords, API keys, secrets and station passwords. Card numbers and IBANs are cut to their last 4 characters. Support drafts, automatic insights, background workers and driver support also mask email addresses and phone numbers, and hash or shorten driver token ids. The assistant sends driver contact details as stored, only to users allowed to read them. Text you type and text files you attach are checked for keys and card numbers. Images and PDFs you attach are sent as they are.

sections.heading: Permissions
sections.text:
| Permission | Allows |
|------------|--------|
| `aiAssistant:read` | Open the assistant and read your past conversations |
| `aiAssistant:write` | Start chats, send messages, attach files, rename and delete conversations, and confirm or reject proposed changes |

By default, administrators have both permissions, operators have both, and viewers have `aiAssistant:read`. A user with read access only sees past conversations and a note that starting a chat needs the write permission. Edit permissions per user on the Users page.

The assistant runs every request as you. Each API call checks your permissions and your site access again, so the assistant cannot reach data or actions you lack.

sections.heading: Open the Assistant
sections.text:
Click the AI button (sparkles icon) in the bottom-right corner of any CSMS page, or press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on macOS). The button appears only when the assistant is turned on and has a provider with an API key, either in Settings or in your personal configuration.

On a wide screen the panel opens on the right side of the page. On a phone it fills the screen.

sections.heading: Ask a Question
sections.text:
1. Type a question in the message box.
2. Press Enter or click Send.
3. The answer streams in as the model writes it. Click Stop to end it early. The partial answer is saved.

The assistant answers in your CSMS language unless you ask for another language. A new chat shows suggested prompts under Try Asking, chosen for the page you are on. Click one to send it.

Example questions:

- "How many stations are online right now?"
- "Show me the top 5 stations by energy delivered this month."
- "How does this week's revenue compare to last week?"
- "List all faulted stations with their error details."

sections.heading: Answers
sections.text:
- Steps: each API call the assistant made appears as a collapsible step with its status and duration.
- Sources: when the answer draws on the EVtivity documentation, a Sources list below the answer links to the documentation pages and sections it cited, in your language when the page has a translation. Answers without such sources show no list.
- Copy: click Copy to copy an answer. Code blocks have their own copy button.
- Answers render tables, lists, and code. Links open in a new tab and only trusted hosts are clickable. Images in answers are not loaded.
- Each answer shows the number of tokens it used.

sections.heading: Keyboard Shortcuts
sections.text:
| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| Ctrl+K or Cmd+K | Open or close the panel |
| Enter | Send the message |
| Shift+Enter | Add a line |
| Up | Put your last message back in the message box (when the box is empty) |
| Esc | Stop the answer, or close the panel when nothing is streaming. A click outside the panel also closes it |

sections.heading: Confirm Changes
sections.text:
The assistant reads data without asking. Any change, such as creating, updating, or deleting a record, stops the answer and shows a Confirm This Change card. The card shows what the change does and its Details.

- Click Confirm to run the change. The assistant then continues its answer.
- Click Reject to cancel it.

The assistant proposes one change at a time. A proposal expires after 5 minutes and then shows Expired. Ask again to get a new one.

Confirming a change needs a signed-in CSMS session. A client that uses an API key can reject a change but cannot confirm it (`AI_CONFIRMATION_REQUIRES_SESSION`).

Some actions are never available to the assistant, even with confirmation: settings and stored secrets, API keys, sign-in and MFA, users and permissions, the AI configuration itself, payments, refunds, invoices, pricing, free vend, station credentials, certificates, network profiles, configuration variables, and firmware. Do these in the CSMS directly.

sections.heading: Explain
sections.text:
An Explain button opens the assistant about one record. It appears on:

- a station that is offline or faulted, in the station header
- a session that failed or faulted
- a refused attempt in the authorize log, on the token, driver, and station pages
- a reservation cancelled because of the station, expired, or with a failed fee, in the reservation header (see Reservation Insights)

The button needs the assistant to be turned on and the `aiAssistant:write` permission.

In a table row, such as the authorize log, the button is an icon. When the record has a current automatic insight, the icon is a light bulb.

1. Click Explain.
2. The panel opens with a context card for the record: the record type and the identifier you know it by, such as Session CS-0954. A station, session, or authorization attempt shows the OCPP station ID, a reservation its number, such as Reservation #12, and an insight its ID.
3. The message box holds a prepared question, such as "Why did this session fail, and what should I do?". Edit it if you like, then send it. Nothing is sent to the AI provider, and no tokens are used, until you send it.

Ask a follow-up on an insight page or on a support case insight opens the assistant about that insight the same way.

The context card stays while the conversation is about the record, also when you open the conversation again from the history. To answer, the assistant reads the record, its events, and its insights with its read tools, under your permissions and site access. New chat starts a conversation without the record.

Press Esc or click outside the panel to close it. Esc first stops an answer that is still streaming. A dialog open above the panel, such as a confirmation, takes Esc and clicks first.

sections.heading: Explain
sections.text:
EVtivity checks your access to the record when the conversation starts and before every answer. When you lose access to the record, the conversation keeps its earlier answers but refuses new questions (`AI_CONTEXT_NOT_FOUND`). The same error answers a record that does not exist or that you cannot see.

What the assistant reads about the record goes to the AI provider, with stored credentials removed and card numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, and token ids masked. A change the assistant suggests still needs your confirmation.

sections.heading: Conversation History
sections.text:
Your conversations are saved and private to you. Open Conversation history in the panel to:

- Search conversations by title.
- Open a conversation to continue it.
- Rename a conversation.
- Delete a conversation and its attachments. This cannot be undone.

Click New chat to start over. Conversations are deleted automatically once they have had no activity for the retention period set in Settings > AI > Usage and Limits (30 days by default).

sections.heading: Attachments
sections.text:
Click Attach files, drop files on the panel, or paste them into the message box. The assistant can read:

- Images (JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF)
- PDF
- CSV, plain text, and log files
- JSON and JSONL (for example, OCPP message traces)

The maximum size and the number of files per message come from the AI limits in Settings (10 MB and 5 files by default). Attachments need S3 storage (see Settings).

Attachments go through the same checks as support case attachments. The server checks each file's content against its declared type and refuses a mismatch. It re-encodes images and removes their metadata (such as location data) before storing them. If the selected model cannot read a file type, the assistant says so instead of answering.

sections.heading: Personal Configuration
sections.text:
You can use your own provider and API key instead of the system settings.

1. Open your Profile page.
2. Open the Chatbot AI tab.
3. Select a Provider and enter your API key.
4. Optionally set a Model (optional), the Effort, and a System prompt (optional).
5. Click Save.

Your configuration applies only to you and takes priority over the system settings. An empty model uses the provider's default model. Click Remove configuration to go back to the system settings.

The tab appears only while the assistant is turned on in Settings. When an administrator turns the assistant off in Settings > AI > Assistant, the AI button disappears and every assistant request is refused, including requests that use a personal configuration.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text:
An administrator sets these in Settings > AI > Usage and Limits. They apply to every user and provider.

- Requests per user per minute: default 10.
- Tokens per user per day: default 2,000,000. 0 means no daily limit. The day runs from midnight to midnight UTC.
- Tool calls per answer: default 20. The assistant stops calling the API for that answer when it reaches the limit.
- Keep conversations for (days): default 30.

Company and site monthly token budgets also apply. See AI Usage and Budgets.

When you reach a limit, the assistant shows an error. Try again later.

The panel footer shows your tokens today against your daily budget.

When the AI provider account of the company is out of credit or quota, the assistant shows the `AI_PROVIDER_QUOTA_EXCEEDED` error until an administrator adds credit or raises the quota at the provider. Administrators see a banner and get a notification. See AI Alerts.

sections.heading: Support Case AI Draft
sections.text:
The AI drafts replies to support cases. It needs the `support:write` permission and Enable support AI in Settings > AI > Support Drafts.

1. Open a support case.
2. Check Internal note for a note to your team. Leave it unchecked for a reply to the customer.
3. Click AI Draft.
4. The draft streams into the message box. Click Stop draft to end it early.
5. Review and edit the draft, then send it yourself.

If the message box already holds text, the CSMS asks before it replaces it. A Sources list below the message box shows the data the AI read for the draft, such as the case, its messages, linked sessions, the station, and the driver.

- A customer reply follows the driver's language. An internal note uses your CSMS language.
- The AI reads only the case and its linked data. It cannot read other cases or other drivers.
- It never changes anything and never sends a message. You decide what to send.

Support AI has its own configuration with a Reply tone (Professional, Friendly, or Formal). Set it in Settings > AI > Support Drafts or, for yourself, on the Support AI tab of your Profile. Support AI requests also count against Support AI requests per site per minute (default 60).

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text:
An automatic insight is a short note about a problem on your network: what probably caused it, how sure the analysis is, how far it reaches, and what to do next. EVtivity creates insights on its own when a station goes offline or reports a fault, when a session fails, when a station refuses a token, or when a reservation fails. You do not have to ask.

Some insights also carry an action that a background AI worker suggests, such as stopping a stuck session. The action runs only when you confirm it (see Insight Actions).

Automatic insights are off by default. An administrator turns them on in Settings > AI > Automatic Insights (see Turn On Automatic Insights).

What the AI Provider Receives

The AI provider never receives stored credentials, such as passwords, API keys, secrets and station passwords. Card numbers and IBANs are cut to their last 4 characters. Support drafts, automatic insights, background workers and driver support also mask email addresses and phone numbers, and hash or shorten driver token ids. The assistant sends driver contact details as stored, only to users allowed to read them. Text you type and text files you attach are checked for keys and card numbers. Images and PDFs you attach are sent as they are.

sections.heading: What Starts an Insight
sections.text:
EVtivity checks for new events once a minute. These events start an insight:

| Event | Insight |
|-------|---------|
| A station disconnects | Station offline |
| A station or one of its connectors reports Faulted | Station faulted |
| A station reports a critical event (an event alert) | Station alert |
| A session ends as failed or faulted | Session failed |
| A station refuses a token | Authorization refused (one per token, station, and hour) |
| A station rejects or does not answer a reservation, or cannot take it at activation | Reservation rejected |
| A reservation expires unused although the station accepted it for a driver | Reservation no-show |
| A station does not cancel a reservation | Reservation cancel failed |
| A reservation fee cannot be charged | Reservation fee failed |
| A reserved station reports a fault during the reservation | Station faulted while reserved |

Reservation events start an insight only while reservations are on (see Reservation Insights). A station that disconnects because the CSMS itself is restarting does not start an insight. Events from before automatic insights were turned on are never analyzed.

Background workers add insights of their own: Stuck session and Station faulted for hours, each with an action, and the Site summary, Network summary, and Tariff anomaly insights. See Background AI Workers.

sections.heading: Wait, Group, and Skip
sections.text:
EVtivity does not analyze every event right away:

1. It waits 2 minutes by default. When the problem clears in that time, for example the station comes back online, the insight ends as Resolved before the analysis and no AI request is made.
2. When 3 or more stations of one site go offline or fault within that wait, they become one Site incident instead of one insight per station. Sessions at a site that fail for the same reason within an hour are grouped the same way, and so are reservation no-shows at a site within an hour. A station faulted while reserved joins the open site incident of its station.
3. When the cause is already known from the data, such as a stop reason or a refusal reason with a fixed meaning, EVtivity writes the insight from its own rules. It is marked Known cause and uses no tokens.
4. A station, session, or token analyzed in the last 60 minutes is not analyzed again (Analyzed recently).
5. Each site gets at most 50 AI-written insights per day.
6. When an AI budget is used up, the insight is stored with the rule-based fields only (see AI Usage and Budgets).

Each of these values is a setting in Settings > AI > Automatic Insights. See Settings.

An insight usually appears 2 to 3 minutes after the event: the scan runs every minute and the analysis waits 2 minutes (Wait before analyzing (seconds), 120 by default). Stations of one site that fail within that wait become one site incident.

sections.heading: Read an Insight
sections.text:
An insight card is labeled Automatic Insight. From top to bottom it shows:

- The insight type, badges such as Known cause, Out of date, or High confidence, and how long ago the insight was created.
- A headline that says what happened and where, the same as on the dashboard card, such as CS-1616 is faulted.
- A short summary written by the AI.
- Likely cause: one of Connectivity, Power supply, Hardware, Firmware, Configuration, Token, Payment, Tariff, Vehicle, Backend, or Unknown.
- Suggested Fix: the steps to take, from a fixed list, such as Check the station's network connection, Reboot the station, or Review the token status. The steps are plain text. When the insight carries an action, the action comes last in this section, with Reject and Confirm (see Insight Actions).
- A footer with Show original, how many users found the insight helpful, and the buttons to act on it (see Act on an Insight).

While an insight is analyzed, the card shows a placeholder of the same shape. An insight that is out of date, was not analyzed, or whose analysis did not finish shows one line with the reason and Regenerate.

The likely cause, confidence, and fixes appear in your CSMS language. The summary is written once in the summary language set in Settings (English by default). When you open an insight in another language, EVtivity translates the summary once and keeps the translation for everyone who reads that language. Until it is ready, the card shows the original with Translating… next to it, and the translation replaces it in place when it arrives, with no reload. When no translation can be made (no provider or a used-up budget), the card shows No translation is available. The original is shown. Click Show original to read the summary in its original language.

sections.heading: Read an Insight
sections.text:
The summary is shown as plain text. Links and formatting in it are not rendered.

An insight that no longer matches the data shows Out of date. When the problem clears, EVtivity marks the insight Resolved.

sections.heading: Statuses
sections.text:
Every insight has one status. It also covers the action the insight carries, if any. The AI Insights list, its Status filter, the dashboard card, and the AI Insights tabs all show this status.

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| Open | The problem needs attention |
| Pending | The insight's action waits for a decision |
| Done | The action was confirmed and ran |
| Rejected | The action was rejected |
| Resolved | The condition cleared on its own: the station came back online or is no longer faulted, or every station of a site incident recovered. A station faulted while reserved resolves when the station is online and no longer faulted, and a reservation fee failure resolves when the fee is captured later. A refused authorization resolves when its cause is gone: the session the card already runs ends, a blocked, expired or unknown card becomes usable, or the same card is accepted later at that station. A stuck session resolves when the session is no longer active, and its offline advice also when the station is back online or the session gets an action. A station alert resolves when the station reports it cleared. Other one-off insights close as expired after Close one-off insights after (days). An action whose condition no longer held when someone confirmed it also resolves its insight |
| Dismissed | A user with the `aiInsights:write` permission dismissed it |
| Expired | Nobody decided on the action before it expired, or a one-off insight (a failed session, a reservation problem, a tariff anomaly, a card refused with no cause the CSMS can watch) stayed open longer than Close one-off insights after (days) |

Done, Rejected, Resolved, Dismissed, and Expired are final. A later event does not change them.

sections.heading: Statuses
sections.text:
The dashboard card shows Open and Pending insights. Station, session, reservation, and site pages list every insight about the record on their AI Insights tab.

While EVtivity analyzes an insight, the card shows Analyzing. An insight that was not analyzed shows the reason, such as Resolved before the analysis, Analyzed recently, the daily limit of the site, insights turned off for the site or in Settings, or a used-up AI budget. When the AI provider fails three times in a row, the card shows The analysis did not finish. An insight replaced by Regenerate, or merged into a site incident or a group of failed sessions, no longer appears in the list.

Out of date is not a status: it marks an insight whose record changed after the analysis. Click Regenerate for a current one.

sections.heading: Where Insights Appear
sections.text:
- Station, session, reservation, and site pages: the AI Insights tab (see AI Insights Tab).
- Support case detail: up to three insights about the case's station and linked sessions. Support AI drafts also read these insights.
- Authorize log (on the token, driver, and station pages): an AI column on refused attempts. Click it to open the insight, or to Explain the attempt when it has none.
- Dashboard: the Active Insights card, below the stat cards (see below).
- AI Insights: the list of all insights (see AI Insights List).

sections.heading: AI Insights Tab
sections.text:
Station, session, reservation, and site pages have an AI Insights tab. It lists every insight about the record, newest first, with the columns Insight, Status, Root Cause, and Created. Click a row to open the insight page. The station tab lists the insights of the station and of its sessions. Reservation insights show only on the reservation page.

A light bulb button floats above the assistant button in the bottom right corner of these pages. Click it to open the AI Insights tab. It shows while the record has an open or pending insight, or one resolved within the last day. It is green and pulses while an insight is open, pulses amber while an action waits for a decision, and shows the number of insights when more than one is open or pending.

The tab and the button need the `aiInsights:read` permission and show only while AI Insights are on. On the reservation page, they show only while reservations are on.

sections.heading: Active Insights Card
sections.text:
The Active Insights card shows below the stat cards of the dashboard, full width. It shows one card per open or pending insight in a row that scrolls sideways: three cards in view on wide screens, two on medium screens, and one on phones. Dots below the row show the scroll position. Click a dot to scroll to it. Each card shows:

- A headline that says what happened and where, such as 3 stations offline at Convention Center or CS-1616 is faulted.
- The status, Open or Pending. Pending marks an insight whose action waits for a decision.
- The root cause, how many stations or sessions are affected, the site, and how long ago it happened.
- A confidence badge, such as High confidence.
- The first suggested fix.

The cards hold no AI-written text. Site incidents come first, then the most severe and newest insights. Insights of the same type and root cause at one site collapse into one card with +N similar. Click a card to open the insight page.
